They then made their way to the border town of Musina, where boys beg on the streets or work on farms, and girls seem to disappear into South African society. UNICEF representative Shantha Bloemen said many Zimbabwean girls either turn to prostitution or work as domestic servants. The United Nations and Save the Children, which has an office based in Musina, report there has been a troubling increase in the number of children under 18 years old who are making the risky journey south from their homes in Zimbabwe to South Africa in search of work and food. Social workers from Save the Children and UNICEF told CNN that in June, 175 Zimbabwean children came over the border illegally and alone. In November, 1,016 kids made the same perilous journey. The boys older than 16 hang around Musina, sleeping on the sidewalk by a sports stadium along with older homeless men. Their days are spent waiting in line, jostling alongside hundreds of Zimbabwean adults, trying to apply for political asylum at a makeshift center opened by South African authorities. A South African official who processes asylum applications says it is common for youngsters to lie about their age so they can get the papers to stay in the country legally. Many, though, cannot get the necessary papers because they do not carry documentation or have adults who can vouch for who they are and where they come from. So, they wander the streets, begging for money. The younger ones like Brian are picked up by police and housed in a safe place until authorities and aid agencies can figure out what to do with them. While they wait for a future that never seems to arrive, boys like Brian and Temashi -- a legacy of Mugabe's regime -- struggle to survive in the world they now find themselves in.

(CNN) — A crude swastika has been carved into Brian’s arm. The dark, threatening-looking mark is not a professional tattoo but a rough design scratched into his skin.

Brian, who is 11, says his 10-year-old friend Temashi used a matchstick over two days to scrape the symbol onto him. Brian said it caused only a little pain. He is among thousands of children from Zimbabwe who have escaped their devastated country, hoping to find a better future in South Africa.

To Brian and his friend, the swastika does not stand for Adolf Hitler, the Holocaust or the atrocities associated with Nazi Germany. They say the sharp, angular symbol on their arms means “Germans never surrender.” However distorted and mistaken that meaning may be, Brian says it gives him courage. Speaking softly, he explained that it shows he is a “man” and “someone who does not surrender.”

Brian and other Zimbabwean children like him are living without adult guardians in an unfamiliar country. Organizations including Save the Children and UNICEF describe them as “unaccompanied minors,” but that official label barely captures the reality of their lives.

These children face extraordinary suffering as they make the journey to South Africa either alone or with small groups of friends. They travel by catching rides on trucks, trains and taxis. Brian and his companions told CNN that when they reached the South African border at Beitbridge, officials allowed them to pass through even though they had no passports or other documents.

From there, they continued to Musina, a town near the border. In Musina, boys can be seen begging in the streets or working on farms, while girls often appear to vanish into South African society. Shantha Bloemen, a UNICEF representative, said many Zimbabwean girls end up in prostitution or become domestic workers.

Almost all of the children — some of them under the age of 10 — leave Zimbabwe because they believe life will be better in South Africa. They cite hunger, schools that no longer function and severe poverty as the reasons for leaving. Many have lost their parents; others still have parents. But they share a deep dislike of President Robert Mugabe’s government, which they say has left them with no real option except to leave home and join the movement south.

Humanitarian organizations say about one-fourth of Zimbabwe’s population has left the country, with most fleeing to nearby South Africa, Botswana and Mozambique.

The United Nations and Save the Children, which operates an office in Musina, say there has been an alarming rise in the number of Zimbabwean children under 18 making the dangerous trip south into South Africa in search of food and work. Social workers from Save the Children and UNICEF told CNN that in June, 175 Zimbabwean children crossed the border illegally and without adults. By November, that number had risen to 1,016.

Older boys, especially those over 16, often remain in Musina, sleeping on pavements near a sports stadium alongside older homeless men. During the day, they wait in long lines with hundreds of Zimbabwean adults at a temporary center set up by South African authorities, hoping to apply for political asylum.

One South African official who handles asylum claims said young people often give false ages so they can obtain papers allowing them to stay legally. Many, however, are unable to secure those documents because they have no identification and no adults who can confirm who they are or where they are from.

As a result, many drift through the streets and beg for money. Younger children, such as Brian, are taken by police to a safe location while authorities and aid groups try to decide what should happen to them.

As they wait for a future that seems endlessly delayed, boys like Brian and Temashi — children shaped by the consequences of Mugabe’s rule — do what they can to stay alive in the harsh world they have entered.

Brian is one of thousands of Zimbabwean children who have left their country in search of a safer and more hopeful future. Many have fled severe poverty, hunger, failing schools, and political hardship in Zimbabwe. For these children, South Africa appears to offer the possibility of food, work, education, or simply survival.

The journey, however, is often dangerous. Many children travel without parents or adult guardians, either alone or in small groups. UNICEF and other charities classify these children as unaccompanied minors. Aid organizations warn that they face severe risks, including homelessness, prostitution, domestic servitude, and other forms of exploitation. ## Alone at the Border: Zimbabwean Children Risk Dangerous Crossings Into South Africa

**MUSINA, South Africa** — Brian is 11 years old, small for his age, and traveling without his parents.

On his arm is a crude swastika tattoo, inked by older boys, he says, during the long journey south. He does not appear to understand its history or meaning. For him, it is just another mark from the road — a road that has taken him from Zimbabwe to the banks of the Limpopo River and toward the South African border town of Musina.

Brian is one of many unaccompanied Zimbabwean children crossing into South Africa through the Beitbridge border area, driven by hunger, family separation, poverty, and the hope of finding work or relatives across the border. Some are fleeing homes where there is little food. Others have lost parents or guardians to illness, migration, or economic collapse. Many travel with little more than the clothes they are wearing.

The crossing is perilous. Children who cannot pass through the official Beitbridge border post often attempt informal routes, moving through bushland, wading across the Limpopo River when water levels allow, or relying on smugglers known locally as “guides.” Along the way, they risk robbery, assault, exploitation, and arrest.

Those who make it to Musina often arrive exhausted, hungry, and frightened.

Aid workers in the town say minors regularly turn up at shelters, police stations, churches, or transit points after days on the road. Some have been separated from adults they were traveling with. Others say they were abandoned by smugglers after paying what little money they had.

“Children are arriving with no documents, no food, and no clear plan,” said one child protection worker in Musina. “Many do not know where they will sleep that night.”

Brian says he left Zimbabwe because there was not enough to eat at home. He hoped to find relatives in South Africa, though he is unsure exactly where they live. Like many children who cross the border alone, his journey is built on fragments of information — a name, a town, a phone number that may no longer work.

In Musina, the first major town south of Beitbridge, the presence of unaccompanied children has become a recurring humanitarian concern. Local services are stretched. Shelters and nonprofit organizations try to provide food, temporary accommodation, counseling, and help tracing family members, but resources are limited.

South African authorities face a difficult task: enforcing immigration laws while also meeting child protection obligations. Under international standards, children traveling alone are supposed to be treated first as vulnerable minors, not simply as undocumented migrants. That means they should be screened for trafficking risks, given access to care, and not returned to dangerous conditions without proper assessment.

But in practice, aid groups say, the system is often overwhelmed.

For children like Brian, the border is not a political line so much as a test of survival. Some hope to find informal jobs despite being far too young to work legally. Others try to continue onward to Johannesburg, Pretoria, or Cape Town, where they believe they may find relatives or opportunity. Along the way, they remain vulnerable to adults who may exploit their desperation.

The swastika on Brian’s arm is a jarring image — a symbol of hate carried by a child who says he does not know what it represents. Aid workers see it instead as evidence of something else: how easily children traveling alone can be influenced, harmed, or marked by those around them.

For now, Brian’s immediate needs are simpler. He wants food. He wants somewhere safe to sleep. And he wants to know whether someone can help him find his family.

At the edge of Musina, trucks continue to roll south from the Beitbridge border post, carrying goods into South Africa. Around them, unseen by many travelers, children continue to arrive — tired, undocumented, and alone — searching for safety on the other side of the border.

## Zimbabwean Child Migrants in South Africa Face Hunger, Poverty and an Uncertain Future

**JOHANNESBURG / MUSINA, South Africa** — At the edge of a crowded taxi rank near South Africa’s border with Zimbabwe, children wait with plastic bags holding the few belongings they carried across the Limpopo River or through official crossing points. Some are with relatives. Some are traveling alone. Many say they came because there was little left for them at home: no money for school, too little food, and families stretched past breaking point.

For years, Zimbabwean children have crossed into South Africa seeking safety, work opportunities, food, education, or family reunification. Their journeys are shaped by a mixture of economic collapse, political history, drought, unemployment and deepening poverty — pressures that have pushed generations of Zimbabweans to look south.

Humanitarian groups warn that children on the move are among the most vulnerable migrants in the region. Without documents, stable shelter or adult protection, they face exploitation, trafficking, abuse, hunger and arrest. Some apply for asylum or other forms of legal protection, while others remain undocumented, fearful of authorities and unable to access basic services.

“Children do not leave home lightly,” humanitarian workers often stress. “When they move alone or in unsafe conditions, it is usually because families have run out of options.”

### Poverty and hunger driving movement

Zimbabwe has endured years of economic instability, marked by high inflation, currency crises, unemployment and recurring food insecurity. In rural areas, droughts and poor harvests have left many households dependent on informal labor, remittances or food assistance. In urban areas, the cost of basic goods has often risen faster than wages.

For children, the consequences can be immediate: empty plates, missed school days, untreated illness and pressure to work.

Families describe making impossible choices — paying school fees for one child while another stays home, sending a teenager to South Africa to look for work, or asking children to live with relatives across the border. Some children migrate after losing parents or caregivers. Others flee family violence, early marriage, or neglect made worse by poverty.

Aid agencies including **UNICEF** have repeatedly warned that economic hardship and food insecurity can intensify risks for children, especially when families are forced to separate. UNICEF has also emphasized the importance of protecting migrant children regardless of their legal status, ensuring access to education, health care, birth registration and social services.

### Dangerous journeys and hidden lives

The route from Zimbabwe into South Africa can be perilous. Some migrants pass through the official Beitbridge border post, one of the busiest crossings in southern Africa. Others use informal routes to avoid documentation checks, crossing rivers, bushland or fenced areas where they risk robbery, assault or extortion.

Children traveling alone are particularly exposed. Humanitarian workers say some are approached by smugglers who promise transport or jobs but later demand payment. Girls may face heightened risk of sexual exploitation. Boys may be pushed into informal labor on farms, in markets, car washes or domestic settings.

Once inside South Africa, many children try to remain invisible. They sleep in overcrowded rooms, informal settlements, abandoned buildings or with distant relatives. Some rely on churches and community groups for food. Others survive through piece jobs, begging or street vending.

For undocumented children, seeking help can feel risky. Fear of deportation, discrimination or being separated from siblings may keep them away from clinics, schools and police stations even when they are sick or in danger.

### Asylum applications and documentation barriers

South Africa has one of the continent’s most developed asylum systems, but it has also faced large backlogs, administrative delays and legal challenges. Zimbabwean adults and children who fear persecution or serious harm may seek asylum, though not all economic migrants qualify under refugee law.

For children, the process is especially complicated. Unaccompanied minors may need social workers, legal guardianship procedures or child protection interventions before their claims can be properly handled. In practice, aid workers say many children do not understand the system, cannot afford transport to refugee reception offices, or lack the documents required to move through bureaucratic channels.

Some Zimbabwean families have relied on temporary permits or special dispensation programs issued by South African authorities over the years, but uncertainty around permit renewals and eligibility has left many households anxious about their future. When parents lack secure documentation, children often suffer too — facing barriers to school enrollment, health care and social protection.

Human rights organizations have urged authorities to ensure that children are not punished for their migration status and that their best interests are prioritized, in line with international child protection standards.

### UNICEF and Save the Children call for protection

UNICEF and **Save the Children** have long worked across southern Africa to support vulnerable children affected by migration, poverty, violence and food insecurity. Their work includes child protection services, family tracing, psychosocial support, access to education, nutrition programs and advocacy for migrant children’s rights.

Save the Children has warned globally that children on the move are at risk of detention, exploitation and being denied essential services. The organization has called for governments to treat migrant children first and foremost as children — not as immigration offenders.

UNICEF has similarly emphasized that every child has the right to protection, education, health care and adequate nutrition, regardless of nationality or legal status. The agency has urged states to keep families together where possible, avoid immigration detention of children, and strengthen cross-border child protection systems.

In border communities, local organizations often serve as the first line of response. They help children contact relatives, report abuse, access clinics, apply for documentation or return home safely when appropriate. But resources are limited, and demand often exceeds capacity.

### The long shadow of Robert Mugabe’s rule

Zimbabwe’s migration crisis cannot be separated from the country’s political and economic history. The late **Robert Mugabe**, who ruled Zimbabwe from independence in 1980 until he was ousted in 2017, remains a central figure in that story.

Mugabe was once celebrated by many as a liberation leader who helped end white minority rule in what was then Rhodesia. But his later decades in power were marked by authoritarianism, violent political repression, controversial land seizures, corruption allegations and economic decline.

The fast-track land reform program launched in 2000 was intended to address colonial-era land inequality, but its chaotic and often violent implementation contributed to a sharp fall in agricultural production and investor confidence. Combined with sanctions, mismanagement, political instability and hyperinflation, the crisis devastated livelihoods.

By the late 2000s, Zimbabwe had experienced one of the worst hyperinflation episodes in modern history. Millions left the country, many heading to South Africa. Teachers, nurses, laborers, farmworkers and entire families crossed the border in search of survival.

Though Mugabe died in 2019, many Zimbabweans say the structural damage of that era remains visible: weakened institutions, limited jobs, underfunded public services and a generation raised amid uncertainty. Current economic challenges have deepened those wounds, leaving children to carry burdens created before they were born.

### School as a lifeline — when children can access it

For migrant children, school can provide more than education. It offers meals, safety, routine and a pathway out of poverty. But enrollment is not always straightforward.

South African law and court rulings have affirmed children’s right to basic education, including undocumented children. Still, families and aid groups report that some schools request documents such as birth certificates, passports, study permits or proof of residence. When parents cannot provide them, children may be turned away or placed on waiting lists.

Language can also be a barrier. Zimbabwean children may speak Shona, Ndebele or other languages at home, while South African classrooms may use English, Afrikaans, isiZulu, Sesotho or other local languages. Children who have missed years of schooling may struggle to catch up.

Some teenagers abandon school altogether to work. They send money home, buy food for siblings or pay rent. But informal jobs often expose them to low wages, abuse and unsafe conditions.

### Hunger in migrant communities

Food insecurity follows many children across the border. In South Africa, undocumented families often cannot access formal social grants. Parents may depend on irregular day labor, domestic work or vending, while rising food prices make it harder to buy staples such as maize meal, cooking oil and beans.

Community kitchens, churches and nongovernmental organizations fill some gaps, but not all. Children may go to bed hungry or rely on school feeding schemes when enrolled. During school holidays, that support can disappear.

Malnutrition is not always visible. Aid workers say children may appear outwardly healthy while suffering from chronic hunger, anemia or developmental delays. Younger children are especially at risk when caregivers cannot afford diverse diets or medical care.

### Xenophobia and fear

Zimbabwean migrants in South Africa also face xenophobia. Periodic outbreaks of anti-immigrant violence have targeted foreign-owned shops and migrant communities. Political rhetoric blaming foreigners for unemployment, crime or pressure on public services has added to fear.

Children absorb that hostility. Some report bullying at school because of their accents or nationality. Others avoid speaking their home language in public. Parents may hesitate to seek police protection after abuse or wage theft because they fear immigration consequences.

South African civil society groups argue that migrants are often scapegoated for deeper structural problems, including unemployment, inequality, housing shortages and weak service delivery.

### A regional responsibility

Experts say child migration between Zimbabwe and South Africa should not be treated solely as a border enforcement issue. It is also a humanitarian, economic and child rights challenge requiring cooperation between governments.

That includes safe migration pathways, stronger asylum and documentation systems, cross-border social services, anti-trafficking measures and investment in communities on both sides of the border.

Zimbabwe’s recovery is central to reducing unsafe migration. Without stable livelihoods, functioning schools, affordable health care and food security, families will continue making desperate decisions.

South Africa, meanwhile, faces the challenge of balancing immigration policy with constitutional and international obligations to protect children.

### “They are children first”

For the children waiting at shelters, bus stations and border towns, policy debates feel distant. Their concerns are immediate: food, safety, school, papers, and whether they will be allowed to stay.

Some dream of becoming nurses, drivers, teachers or engineers. Others simply want to reunite with parents they have not seen in years. Many carry memories of hunger and hardship but also hope that South Africa might offer a chance at stability.

Humanitarian agencies say that hope must be met with protection.

Whether a child crossed a river, arrived at a border post, applied for asylum or entered without documents, advocates say the principle should be the same: no child should be left hungry, unprotected or invisible.

As one child protection worker in the region put it: “Migration status does not erase childhood. These children need safety before anything else.”

counterfactuals.output:
The first thing 15-year-old Tawanda shows a visitor is not the place where he sleeps, or the thin plastic bag that holds all he owns, but a scar on his forearm.

It is a crude swastika, scratched into his skin with a safety pin by another Zimbabwean boy during their first weeks in Johannesburg.

“He said it was a sign for people who survive,” Tawanda says quietly, turning his arm so the raised lines catch the light. “I didn’t know what it was.”

Only later did a church volunteer explain that the swastika is best known worldwide as the emblem of Nazi Germany — a symbol associated with Adolf Hitler, antisemitism, white supremacy and the murder of six million Jews during the Holocaust. In many places, it remains a mark of hatred and racial terror.

For Tawanda and other young Zimbabweans living on the margins of South African cities, the symbol had arrived stripped of its history and remade by rumor. Some believed it meant toughness. Others said it was a gang mark. A few had seen it scratched on walls or tattooed on older boys and understood only that it was meant to frighten.

“To us, it meant: don’t touch me,” says Blessing, 16, who crossed the border alone last year. “It meant you are dangerous, even if you are just a child.”

Across South Africa, aid workers say growing numbers of Zimbabwean minors are arriving without parents or guardians, pushed south by economic collapse, hunger, family breakdown and the hope of finding work. They cross by bus, truck, on foot and, for the poorest and most desperate, through the bush near the Limpopo River — a journey shadowed by smugglers, thieves, police, hunger and the threat of assault.

Many leave without telling anyone.

Tawanda says he walked out of his grandmother’s home near Masvingo after three days without a proper meal. His mother had gone to South Africa years earlier and stopped sending money. His father, he says, “is somewhere else.” A neighbor gave him the phone number of a man who could “help children cross.”

By the time Tawanda reached Beitbridge, the border town linking Zimbabwe and South Africa, he had sold his shoes for transport money and was traveling with two other boys he had met on the road. They crossed at night with a group led by men who demanded extra payment halfway through.

“If you had no money, they beat you,” he says. “One boy was left behind.”

The boys who make it to Johannesburg often find themselves in a second, longer journey: surviving a city that sees them as foreigners, children and workers all at once. Some sleep in parks, taxi ranks or abandoned buildings. Some wash cars, carry groceries, load trucks or beg near traffic lights. Others are pulled into informal networks controlled by older youths who offer protection in exchange for money, obedience or participation in petty crime.

“They are children, but they quickly learn not to look like children,” says a social worker at a migrant shelter in central Johannesburg. “They grow hard faces. They use symbols, slang, scars, anything that gives them a little power.”

South Africa has long been a destination for Zimbabweans fleeing political violence and economic hardship, but unaccompanied minors occupy a particularly precarious place. Without documents, they struggle to enroll in school, access health care or approach police when abused. Even those with a legal claim to protection often do not know how to make it.

Some fear deportation. Others fear being sent back to relatives who cannot feed them.

“I came to work,” says 17-year-old Farai, who left Bulawayo after his uncle told him there was no money for school fees. “If I go home, I am still hungry. If I stay here, maybe I can eat.”

Farai sleeps behind a market stall and earns small change helping vendors unload produce before dawn. He keeps a torn notebook in his pocket, filled with English words he copies from signs. He says he wants to return to school, but cannot see how.

At night, he says, the younger boys cluster together for safety. They warn one another about police raids, violent street groups and employers who refuse to pay. They also trade stories — some true, some exaggerated — about signs and markings that might protect them.

That is how the swastika reached Tawanda’s arm.

His friend, an older boy from Mutare, had seen the symbol on another youth and believed it carried power. One evening, while the group sat behind a closed shop, he used a pin to cut the shape into Tawanda’s skin and rubbed ash into the wound so it would scar.

Tawanda says he did not cry. Crying, he had learned, invites ridicule.

Now he wishes he had refused.

“When they told me what it means, I felt bad,” he says. “I don’t hate those people. I don’t even know those people.”

The misunderstanding troubles educators who work with migrant children. They say it reflects not only the boys’ vulnerability but also their isolation from schooling, family guidance and basic historical knowledge. A symbol of organized hatred can become, in the hands of frightened children, a badge of imagined protection.

“They are trying to create armor,” says the social worker. “But they are using the language of violence because violence is what they have been taught to understand.”

For many South Africans, undocumented migrants have become targets of anger over unemployment, crime and failing public services. Periodic outbreaks of xenophobic violence have left foreign nationals beaten, displaced or killed. Zimbabwean children traveling alone learn quickly to hide their accents, avoid certain neighborhoods and say as little as possible when confronted.

Tawanda says he tells strangers he is from Limpopo Province, not Zimbabwe. He has practiced South African phrases. He lowers his eyes when adults speak to him.

Still, he dreams of ordinary things: a school uniform, a bed, a phone call from his mother. He says he would like to become a mechanic. He likes engines because “if you know the problem, you can fix it.”

Asked what he will do about the mark on his arm, he pulls down his sleeve.

“Maybe one day I remove it,” he says. “Or maybe I just grow and it becomes small.”

For now, the scar remains — not a sign of ideology, but of confusion, fear and the strange codes children invent when they are forced to navigate adult dangers alone. To the world, the swastika is a warning from history. To Tawanda, it is a reminder of a night behind a shop in Johannesburg, when a boy far from home believed that being marked as dangerous might make him safe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a serious international news piece on children fleeing Zimbabwe because of poverty and failed schools, covering their dangerous journey, life on the streets in South Africa, and how charities classify them as unaccompanied minors.
counterfactuals.output:
**Children flee Zimbabwe’s poverty and failing schools, only to face danger on South Africa’s streets**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*Musina/Johannesburg, South Africa*

For many children leaving Zimbabwe, the journey begins with a quiet decision made in hunger: there is no food at home, no money for school fees, no teacher in the classroom, and little hope that tomorrow will be different.

Some leave with the blessing of desperate relatives. Others slip away without telling anyone. They travel south toward South Africa, often alone or in small groups, hoping to find work, food, schooling or family members who crossed before them. Many are not yet teenagers.

Their route is dangerous. Children heading for South Africa’s northern border often pass through Beitbridge, one of the region’s busiest crossing points, or attempt informal routes across the Limpopo River and surrounding bush. Along the way, they risk robbery, assault, sexual exploitation, drowning, and abuse by smugglers or criminal gangs known locally as *magumaguma*, who prey on migrants moving through the borderlands.

Those who survive the crossing often arrive in Musina, the first major South African town beyond the border, exhausted, hungry and without documents. Some continue to Johannesburg, Pretoria or Cape Town. Many end up sleeping near taxi ranks, markets, bus stations, construction sites or under bridges, surviving through begging, informal work, or the support of churches and charities.

Humanitarian groups say these children are part of a wider movement of Zimbabweans driven by years of economic instability, unemployment, food insecurity and deteriorating public services. Zimbabwe’s education system, once among the strongest in Africa, has been weakened by teacher shortages, poor pay, unaffordable fees, and families’ inability to cover uniforms, books and transport. In rural areas and poorer townships, children may attend classes irregularly or drop out entirely.

For children, migration is often framed as survival.

Aid workers in South Africa say they regularly meet Zimbabwean children who have crossed the border without a parent or legal guardian. Under child-protection standards, charities and social workers classify them as **unaccompanied minors** — a designation that recognises their vulnerability and their need for special protection, shelter, tracing of family members, legal assistance and access to schooling.

But classification does not guarantee safety. South Africa’s child-protection system is overstretched, and undocumented migrant children can fall through gaps between immigration enforcement, social services and local shelters. Some avoid officials because they fear deportation or detention. Others are too young to explain where they came from or how to contact relatives.

On the streets, children face new forms of danger. Older migrants or criminal groups may exploit them for cheap labour, street vending, begging or sex. Boys are often drawn into informal car-guarding, loading goods at markets, recycling scrap or working on farms. Girls may be especially vulnerable to sexual abuse and coercion. Without papers, many children struggle to enrol in school or access healthcare, despite legal protections that should allow children to receive basic services regardless of nationality.

Charities working near the border say the children’s stories are strikingly similar: a grandmother left caring for too many dependents; a mother who migrated and stopped sending money; a school demanding fees the family could not pay; a household surviving on one meal a day. Some children say they came to South Africa to find relatives. Others say simply that they came because there was nothing left at home.

The journey also leaves psychological scars. Social workers report cases of trauma, anxiety, substance abuse and depression among children who have been robbed, beaten or assaulted during the crossing. Many have spent months or years without stable adult care. Some do not know whether their parents are alive.

Governments in the region have long struggled to manage cross-border child migration. Zimbabwe’s economic pressures push children out, while South Africa’s stronger economy — despite its own high unemployment and rising anti-migrant sentiment — continues to draw them in. Periodic crackdowns on undocumented migrants can drive children further underground, making them harder for aid groups to reach.

Child-rights organisations argue that the response must begin with protection, not punishment. They call for safe reporting mechanisms, temporary documentation, access to schools, properly funded shelters, and cross-border systems to reunite children with families when it is safe to do so. They also stress that returns to Zimbabwe should be carefully assessed, because sending a child back to extreme poverty, neglect or abuse may place them at renewed risk.

At the heart of the crisis is a grim calculation made by children far too young to make it: whether the dangers of leaving are worse than the hardship of staying.

For those sleeping on South African streets, the answer remains uncertain. They have escaped empty classrooms and empty cupboards, but many have not found safety. They have crossed a border, yet remain suspended between two systems — children in need of care, protection and a future, but too often treated first as migrants, and only later as children.
